deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page lists properties of rings of (semi-)invariants: (1) invariance under certain linear transformations of the coefficients, and conversely; (2) annihilation by linear differential operators, and conversely. This page continues the list and then abstracts it.

The list, in modern terms. Let S be a set of polynomials in k[x_1..x_n] with k = C.
(1) S is the set of polynomials invariant under some group G of linear substitutions, and conversely.
(2) S is the common kernel of a family of linear differential operators (derivations), and conversely.
(3) S is closed under + and - and also under products. So S is a subring, an 'Integritätsbereich'.
(4) S is algebraically closed inside the polynomial ring. If F is a polynomial and F is algebraic over S (more generally an analytic function of elements of S), then F lies in S. Equivalently S = L ∩ k[x], where L is a subfield of k(x) algebraically closed in k(x). [This reformulation is mine.]
(5) S is factorially closed: if AB lies in S, then A and B lie in S.
(6) S is finitely generated: S = k[f_1..f_m] for finitely many f_i.

Definition. A system of polynomials with property (4) is a 'volles Formensystem (in erweitertem Sinne)'.

Research programme sketched (no proofs are given on the page):
(a) Every element of a full system is a rational function of finitely many of its elements. This means Frac(S) is finitely generated, which is true because subfields of a finitely generated field are finitely generated.
(b) Every full system has properties 1, 2, 3 and 6.
(c) Ask under which conditions property 5 holds.
(d) Hope that each of the six properties follows from any other, above all that all follow from (4). The sentence ends on the next page.

The next page applies the idea: to solve f = a, g = b, ..., take as new unknowns the finite basis of the full system generated by f, g, ....

This is a direct precursor of Hilbert's 14th problem (1900): is L ∩ k[x] finitely generated for a subfield L of k(x)?
errors: Not an error on the page, but the hoped-for implication (4) => (6) is false in general. Nagata (1959) gave the counterexample: the invariant ring of a connected vector group. Its invariant field is algebraically closed in k(x), so the ring has property 4, yet it is not finitely generated. Zariski (1954) proved finiteness only when trdeg L <= 2.

(4) does not imply (5). Example: S = C[xy] is full, since C(xy) is algebraically closed in C(x,y). But xy lies in S while x does not. Hilbert himself leaves (5) open, so this is consistent with the page.

(4) does not imply (1) in the linear-group sense: not every algebraically closed subring is a ring of invariants of a linear group. Property (2), constants of derivations, does hold in characteristic 0. The reason is that an algebraically closed subfield L of a finitely generated K is the field of constants of Der_L(K).
Claim (a) is correct, since every subfield of a finitely generated field extension is finitely generated. Claim (b) is false as stated for properties 1 and 6.

results.what: Abstract list of structural properties of invariant rings: subring, algebraically closed in k[x], factorially closed, finitely generated, kernel of derivations, fixed ring of linear group
results.modern_name: Algebraically closed / factorially closed subalgebras of polynomial rings; rings of invariants; kernels of derivations
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (14th problem, 1900); later Zariski, Nagata; factorially closed subrings in the modern affine algebraic geometry literature

results.what: Definition of 'volles Formensystem in erweitertem Sinne' as a polynomial set closed under algebraic dependence (S = L ∩ k[x])
results.modern_name: Rings of the form L ∩ k[x_1..x_n] in Hilbert's 14th problem

results.what: Conjecture that property 4 implies finite generation (6) and the other properties
Full system's elements are rational functions of finitely many of them
results.modern_name: Finite generation of subfields of finitely generated fields

deep.surprise_reason: The 14th problem itself is Hilbert's, so the core idea is known to be his. The page documents an unpublished, programmatic precursor: the algebraic-closure property (4), factorial closedness (5) and the explicit hope that finite generation follows from (4). This is a notable glimpse of the genesis of the 14th problem, but not a new result.
